title: Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 22: Security Logging, Monitoring, and Incident Response. It builds practical understanding of Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity turns a security intention into evidence, an operational owner, and a repeatable control. Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation.

content_blocks.title: Visual model: Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-stage visual model for Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity: Capture security event; Redact sensitive values; Correlate signals; Respond + retest.
content_blocks.caption: Concept map for Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity. It is a learning aid, not a substitute for the stated control conditions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity can be understood through this sequence: Capture security event → Redact sensitive values → Correlate signals → Respond + retest. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 167.1 Backup confidentiality and integrity; 167.2 Recovery-point and recovery-time objectives; 167.3 Restore testing; 167.4 Disaster recovery procedures; 167.5 Recovery verification and lessons learned. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity
content_blocks.code:
Topic: Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity
Review artifact: define scope, assumptions, control owner, expected secure behavior, failure behavior, and a reproducible verification step.
content_blocks.expected_output: A written review artifact names the control and the evidence needed to verify it.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local/owned application or explicitly authorized test target. Record only sanitized synthetic evidence; use human review for behavior that a static snippet cannot prove.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Backup, Recovery, and Business Continuity is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
